---
title: "BIOS 667 Hands-On Session 1"
subtitle: "From raw longitudinal data to valid inference (Ch. 1-4)"
author: "David Zhang"
format:
  live-html:
    toc: true
    include-after-body:
      text: |
        <script>
        // "Run all above": fill every earlier code box with its correct code
        // (exercise boxes get their Solution code) and run them, top to bottom.
        (function() {
          var POLL = 25;          // ms between readiness polls
          var QUIET = 5;          // consecutive idle polls that mean "settled"
          var MAX_START = 10000;  // ms to wait for a click to start a run
          var MAX_RUN = 150000;   // ms cap on a single cell
          var DNONE = /(^|\s)d-none(\s|$)/;

          function allCells() {
            return Array.prototype.slice.call(
              document.querySelectorAll("div.cell[data-caption]"));
          }
          function liveCells() {
            return allCells().filter(function(c) { return c.querySelector(".cm-content"); });
          }
          function viewOf(cell) {
            return cell.querySelector(".cm-content").cmView.view;
          }
          // The cell's own source, decoded from the payload the extension embeds.
          // Reading it here (rather than from the editor at startup) means a
          // student's edits can never be mistaken for the original code.
          function sourceCode(cell) {
            var s = cell.querySelector('script[type$="-contents"]');
            if (!s) return null;
            try {
              var bin = atob(s.textContent.replace(/\s+/g, ""));
              var bytes = Uint8Array.from(bin, function(ch) { return ch.charCodeAt(0); });
              return JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(bytes)).code;
            } catch (e) { return null; }
          }
          // Exercise cells carry data-exercise, so the solution is matched by id
          // rather than by document position.
          function solutionCode(cell) {
            var id = cell.getAttribute("data-exercise");
            if (!id) return null;
            var code = document.querySelector(
              '.exercise-solution[data-exercise="' + id + '"] pre code');
            return code ? code.textContent.replace(/\n$/, "") : null;
          }
          function correctCode(cell) {
            return solutionCode(cell) || sourceCode(cell);
          }

          // Completion tracking. A cell's eval indicator loses d-none while it
          // runs and regains it when it stops, but those windows can be under
          // 20 ms, so polling the class misses them entirely. A MutationObserver
          // sees every transition, and counting the hidden -> shown ones gives a
          // monotone tally of how many times this cell has started running.
          var seen = new WeakMap();
          function track(cell) {
            if (seen.has(cell)) return seen.get(cell);
            var spinner = cell.querySelector(".exercise-editor-eval-indicator");
            var s = { starts: 0, spinner: spinner };
            seen.set(cell, s);
            if (spinner) {
              new MutationObserver(function(recs) {
                recs.forEach(function(r) {
                  if (DNONE.test(r.oldValue || "")) s.starts++;
                });
              }).observe(spinner, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["class"],
                                    attributeOldValue: true });
            }
            return s;
          }
          function anyBusy() {
            return Array.prototype.some.call(
              document.querySelectorAll(".exercise-editor-eval-indicator"),
              function(sp) { return !DNONE.test(sp.getAttribute("class") || ""); });
          }
          // Run one cell and resolve once it has both started and gone quiet.
          // Exercise cells evaluate twice per click, so we require a run of
          // consecutive idle polls rather than the first idle reading.
          function runCell(cell) {
            var s = track(cell);
            var before = s.starts;
            var btn = cell.querySelector('a[aria-label="Run Code"]');
            if (btn) btn.click();
            return new Promise(function(resolve) {
              var t0 = Date.now(), quiet = 0;
              (function poll() {
                var waited = Date.now() - t0;
                var began = !s.spinner || s.starts > before;
                quiet = (began && !anyBusy()) ? quiet + 1 : 0;
                if (quiet >= QUIET || waited > MAX_RUN ||
                    (!began && waited > MAX_START)) { resolve(); return; }
                setTimeout(poll, POLL);
              })();
            });
          }

          var running = false;
          function setBusy(on) {
            running = on;
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(
              document.querySelectorAll('a[aria-label="Run all above"]'),
              function(a) { a.classList.toggle("disabled", on); });
          }
          async function runAllAbove(cell) {
            if (running) return;
            setBusy(true);
            var label = cell.querySelector(
              'a[aria-label="Run all above"] .btn-label-exercise-editor');
            var text = label ? label.textContent : null;
            try {
              var cells = liveCells();
              var stop = cells.indexOf(cell);
              for (var j = 0; j < stop; j++) {
                if (label) label.textContent = "Running " + (j + 1) + "/" + stop;
                var code = correctCode(cells[j]);
                if (code !== null) {
                  var v = viewOf(cells[j]);
                  v.dispatch({ changes: { from: 0, to: v.state.doc.length, insert: code } });
                }
                await runCell(cells[j]);
              }
            } finally {
              if (label) label.textContent = text;
              setBusy(false);
            }
          }

          function addButton(cell) {
            var startOver = cell.querySelector('a[aria-label="Start Over"]');
            var grp = startOver ? startOver.parentElement
                                : cell.querySelector(".btn-group-exercise-editor");
            if (!grp || grp.querySelector('[aria-label="Run all above"]')) return;
            var a = document.createElement("a");
            a.className = "d-flex align-items-center gap-1 btn btn-exercise-editor " +
                          "btn-outline-dark btn-sm text-nowrap";
            a.setAttribute("role", "button");
            a.tabIndex = 0;
            a.setAttribute("aria-label", "Run all above");
            var span = document.createElement("span");
            span.className = "btn-label-exercise-editor";
            span.textContent = "Run all above";
            a.appendChild(span);
            a.addEventListener("click", function() { runAllAbove(cell); });
            grp.prepend(a);
          }
          // Only offer the button once webR is live: every cell has an editor
          // and every Run Code button has come out of its disabled state.
          function init() {
            var cells = liveCells();
            var runs = document.querySelectorAll('a[aria-label="Run Code"]');
            var ready = cells.length === allCells().length && runs.length === cells.length &&
              Array.prototype.every.call(runs, function(r) {
                return !r.classList.contains("disabled");
              });
            if (!ready) { setTimeout(init, 250); return; }
            cells.forEach(function(c, i) {
              track(c);
              if (i > 0) addButton(c);
            });
          }
          init();
        })();
        </script>
engine: knitr
webr:
  packages:
    - dplyr
    - tidyr
    - ggplot2
    - nlme
  resources:
    - data/dental.txt
  cell-options:
    timelimit: 120
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height: 5
live:
  show-hints: true
  show-solutions: true
---

## How this page works

Every gray box below is a live R console running **in your browser**. Nothing is
installed on your computer. When the page finishes loading (the status line under
the first box reads "Run code"), you can type in any box and press
**Run Code** (or Ctrl/Cmd + Enter).

Follow-along boxes are pre-filled: run them and read them. **Exercise** boxes
give you instructions and `NULL` placeholders; replace each `NULL` with your
own code, trying hints before the solution. Nothing runs until you click, and later boxes use objects
made by earlier ones, so **run the boxes top to bottom**.

Later boxes use the objects your own code creates, so an exercise must succeed
before you move on. Stuck, or joining late? Every box after the first has a
**Run all above** button: it fills every earlier box with its correct code
(exercises get their solution) and runs them all, so you can always catch up to
the class in one click. It does not run the box itself, and it appears only once
the page has finished loading.

If you did not run the pre-class test from the email, do it now:

```{webr}
#| caption: "[0A] Test cell: run me first"
R.version.string
plot(1:10, main = "If you can see this plot, you are ready")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
If the box never becomes runnable, or the plot does not appear: reload the page
once, and if it still fails, raise your hand. You can pair up with a neighbor for
today; the page keeps working on any modern browser and on tablets.
:::

Prefer your own R or RStudio instead? Download the script version of this
session, [HandsOn_Session1.R](HandsOn_Session1.R){download="HandsOn_Session1.R"},
which contains the same code, the exercise prompts, and the worked solutions
(it fetches the dataset for you on first run).

**Notation for today** (all introduced in Ch. 1-4): $Y_{ij}$ is the response for
subject $i$ at occasion $j$, with $N$ subjects and $n_i$ occasions each. The mean
model is $E(Y_{ij}) = X_{ij}\beta$, and the covariance of the response vector is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{Y}_i) = \Sigma_i$.

# Problem 1: The dental growth data

Twenty-seven children, each measured at ages 8, 10, 12 and 14 (Potthoff and
Roy, 1964), the running example of FLW Ch. 5, 7 and 8. Six sections take it from
a raw text file to a defensible inference, and then break it on purpose to watch
a missing-data mechanism create bias.

## Section 1: Load and reshape the data

The dental growth data (Potthoff and Roy, 1964) is the running example of
FLW Ch. 5, 7, and 8. The file is already loaded into this page's virtual
filesystem at `data/dental.txt`.

About the raw file:

- the first 27 lines are a **comment header**, not data, and
- the data is in **wide** format: one row per child, one column per age.

Run the follow-along cell:

```{webr}
#| caption: "[1A] Follow along: load the raw (wide) data"
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(nlme)

dental_raw <- read.table("data/dental.txt", header = FALSE, skip = 27,
                         col.names = c("id", "gender",
                                       "age8", "age10", "age12", "age14"))
head(dental_raw)
```

```{webr}
#| caption: "[1B] Follow along: how many children of each gender?"
table(dental_raw$gender)
```

### Task 1: wide to long

Most longitudinal tools in R expect **long** format: one row per (child, age)
pair, that is, one row per $Y_{ij}$. Write the reshape yourself.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_reshape
#| envir: global
#| caption: "[1C] Task 1: wide to long"
# Reshape dental_raw from wide to long with pivot_longer():
#   - gather the four measurement columns (age8, age10, age12, age14)
#   - their names should go into a column called "visit"
#   - their values should go into a column called "distance"
# Assign the result to `dental_long`.

# Replace NULL with your code:
dental_long <- NULL

head(dental_long, 8)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_reshape"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

The skeleton is `dental_long <- dental_raw |> pivot_longer(cols = ..., names_to = ..., values_to = ...)`.
Select the four measurement columns with `starts_with("age")`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_reshape"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

```r
dental_long <- dental_raw |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("age"),
               names_to = ______,
               values_to = ______)
```

Both blanks are quoted column names.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_reshape"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
dental_long <- dental_raw |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("age"),
               names_to = "visit",
               values_to = "distance")

head(dental_long, 8)
```

Each child now contributes 4 rows, so `dental_long` has $27 \times 4 = 108$ rows.
:::
:::

Now polish YOUR `dental_long` into the analysis data `dental`: two cosmetic
steps you do not need to write yourself, turning `"age8"` into the number 8 and
giving `gender` readable labels. This box only works once Task 1 has run.

```{webr}
#| caption: "[1D] Follow along: tidy the long data (numeric age, labeled gender)"
dental <- dental_long |>
  mutate(age = as.numeric(gsub("age", "", visit)),
         gender = factor(gender, levels = c("F", "M"),
                         labels = c("Girl", "Boy")))
nrow(dental)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 1

1. Why does `read.table()` need `skip = 27` here? What would happen without it?
2. Give one concrete reason long format is preferred for modeling.
:::

## Section 2: See the data before modeling it

### The spaghetti plot

Run the cell as given. Two pieces carry the statistical content: `group = id`
connects the points belonging to the same child, the visual analog of "rows
sharing an `id` are not independent", and `stat_summary(fun = mean)` lays one
mean curve per gender over the individual trajectories.

```{webr}
#| caption: "[2A] Follow along: spaghetti plot with group means"
ggplot(dental, aes(x = age, y = distance, group = id, color = gender)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = gender), fun = mean,
               geom = "line", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(title = "Dental growth: individual trajectories and group means",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Distance (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 2

Look at the plot and answer in plain words:

1. What is the overall growth pattern, and do boys and girls look different?
2. "Tracking": do children keep their rank over time? What feature of the plot
   tells you?
3. Which looks bigger here: variability *between* children or *within* a child
   over time?
:::

## Section 3: Quantify the correlation

### Task 3: the correlation matrix

The wide format earns its keep here: each age is a column, so the whole
$4 \times 4$ correlation matrix across occasions is one function call.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cor
#| envir: global
#| caption: "[3A] Task 3: the correlation matrix"
# Compute the correlation matrix of the four measurement columns of
# dental_raw (age8, age10, age12, age14), rounded to 2 decimal places.
# Assign it to `cor_mat`.

# Replace NULL with your code:
cor_mat <- NULL

cor_mat
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cor"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`cor()` applied to a data frame with several numeric columns returns the full
correlation matrix. Select the four columns by name from `dental_raw`, and wrap
the result in `round(..., 2)`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cor"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

```r
cor_mat <- round(cor(dental_raw[, c(______)]), 2)
```

The blank is a vector of four quoted column names.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_cor"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
cor_mat <- round(cor(dental_raw[, c("age8", "age10", "age12", "age14")]), 2)
cor_mat
```
:::
:::

Now run the follow-along heatmap. Note the orientation: the top-left cell is the
(age8, age8) entry, exactly as the matrix prints.

```{webr}
#| caption: "[3B] Follow along: correlation heatmap (printed-matrix orientation)"
cor_mat <- round(cor(dental_raw[, c("age8", "age10", "age12", "age14")]), 2)
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat))
names(cor_long) <- c("row", "col", "r")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = col, y = row, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 4) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(levels(cor_long$row))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#4B9CD3", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation of dental distance across ages",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 3

1. How strong is the within-child correlation, roughly?
2. Recall the two working patterns from Ch. 2: compound symmetry (one common
   correlation at every lag) and AR(1) (correlation decays geometrically with
   lag). Which does this matrix resemble more?
3. What does your answer suggest for the model we fit next?
:::

## Section 4: Why OLS is not enough

OLS treats all 108 rows as independent. We just measured correlations around
0.6 to 0.8, so that assumption is plainly false. The mean model can still be
right, and $\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}$ is still unbiased, but the reported standard
errors are computed under the wrong covariance, so the *inference* is invalid.

### Task 4: fit both models

This is the model-fitting skill of the day, so you write both calls yourself.
The mean model is the same both times: distance depends on age and gender.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_gls
#| envir: global
#| caption: "[4A] Task 4: fit both models"
# 1. Fit the mean model  distance ~ age + gender  by OLS with lm().
#    Call the fit `ols`.
# 2. Fit the SAME mean model with gls() from nlme, adding a
#    compound-symmetry correlation within each child (grouping variable: id).
#    Call the fit `gls_cs`. The last line prints its coefficient table.

# Replace each NULL with your code:
ols <- NULL
gls_cs <- NULL

if (is.null(ols) || is.null(gls_cs)) stop("Replace the NULLs above with your code.")
summary(gls_cs)$tTable
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_gls"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`gls()` takes the same formula and `data` as `lm()`, plus a `correlation`
argument. Compound symmetry within child is `corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id)`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_gls"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

```r
ols <- lm(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental)

gls_cs <- gls(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental,
              correlation = ______)

summary(gls_cs)$tTable
```

The blank is the `corCompSymm(...)` call. Pass the grouping formula as the
**named** `form` argument: if you write `corCompSymm(~ 1 | id)` without
`form =`, the formula lands in the wrong argument slot and **no** working
correlation is fit, silently.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_gls"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ols <- lm(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental)

gls_cs <- gls(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental,
              correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))

summary(gls_cs)$tTable
```
:::
:::

Now compare the standard errors of your two fits side by side:

```{webr}
#| caption: "[4B] Follow along: the SE comparison"
se_ols <- coef(summary(ols))[, "Std. Error"]
se_gls <- summary(gls_cs)$tTable[, "Std.Error"]
round(cbind(OLS = se_ols, GLS_CS = se_gls, ratio = se_gls / se_ols), 3)
```

```{webr}
#| caption: "[4C] Follow along: the estimated within-child correlation"
coef(gls_cs$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 4: the punchline of the whole session

Look at the `ratio` column.

1. Which coefficient's standard error got **larger** once correlation was
   modeled, and which got **smaller**?
2. Explain both directions. (Hint: gender is constant within a child; age varies
   within a child.)
3. Complete the sentence: "Ignoring positive within-subject correlation makes
   OLS standard errors ______."
:::

## Section 5: ML vs REML, and a real test

Ch. 4 gives us two likelihood-based estimators. **REML** corrects the downward
bias of ML variance estimates (the same idea as dividing a sample variance by
$n - p$ instead of $n$) and is the default for reported fits. But REML
log-likelihoods of models with **different mean structures are not comparable**,
so a likelihood ratio test comparing mean models must use **ML**.

Question from the spaghetti plot: do boys and girls grow at different **rates**?
That is the `age:gender` interaction.

### Task 5: LRT for the interaction

You know every ingredient from Task 4, and the one new decision is the
estimation method.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_lrt
#| envir: global
#| caption: "[5A] Task 5: LRT for the interaction"
# 1. Fit the additive model      distance ~ age + gender   with gls(),
#    compound-symmetry correlation within child, and THE METHOD THAT MAKES
#    MEAN-MODEL LIKELIHOODS COMPARABLE. Call it `m_add`.
# 2. Fit the interaction model   distance ~ age * gender   the same way.
#    Call it `m_int`.
# The last line compares the two fits: the likelihood ratio test.

# Replace each NULL with your code:
m_add <- NULL
m_int <- NULL

if (is.null(m_add) || is.null(m_int)) stop("Replace the NULLs above with your code.")
anova(m_add, m_int)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_lrt"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

The method is ML, requested with `method = "ML"` in **both** `gls()` calls.
`distance ~ age * gender` expands to age, gender, and age:gender.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_lrt"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

```r
m_add <- gls(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental,
             correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), method = ______)

m_int <- gls(distance ~ ______, data = dental,
             correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), method = ______)

anova(m_add, m_int)
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_lrt"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
m_add <- gls(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental,
             correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), method = "ML")

m_int <- gls(distance ~ age * gender, data = dental,
             correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), method = "ML")

anova(m_add, m_int)
```

The LRT statistic is about 6.2 on 1 df, p = 0.013: the growth rates differ.
:::
:::

Having chosen the mean model with ML, refit it with REML (the default) to report:

```{webr}
#| caption: "[5B] Follow along: final model, REML fit for reporting"
m_final <- gls(distance ~ age * gender, data = dental,
               correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
round(summary(m_final)$tTable, 3)
```

```{webr}
#| caption: "[5C] Follow along: ML vs REML residual SD on the additive model"
c(ML = gls(distance ~ age + gender, data = dental,
           correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), method = "ML")$sigma,
  REML = gls_cs$sigma)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 5

1. Why did the LRT require `method = "ML"`?
2. From the REML table: what is the girls' growth rate, and what is the boys'?
3. Which residual SD came out smaller, ML or REML, and why is that the expected
   direction?
:::

## Section 6: A live missing-data experiment

The dental data is complete, which makes it perfect for an experiment: we know
the truth, so we can *watch* a missing-data mechanism create bias.

**The story.** Suppose the age-14 visit had been skipped for every child whose
age-12 distance was 26 mm or more (say the orthodontist referred them to a
specialist and they left the study).

```{webr}
#| caption: "[6A] Follow along: apply the dropout rule"
wide <- dental_raw
wide$dropout <- wide$age12 >= 26
table(dropout = wide$dropout)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 6a: name that mechanism

Dropout depends only on the age-12 measurement, which was recorded for everyone.
Is this MCAR, MAR, or MNAR? Vote before expanding.
:::

### Task 6: measure the damage

Compare the age-14 mean computed from all 27 children (the truth, which we only
know because this is an experiment) with the mean a naive analyst would compute
from the completers only. `wide` has columns `age14` (numeric) and `dropout`
(logical).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mar
#| envir: global
#| caption: "[6B] Task 6: measure the damage"
# 1. Compute the age-14 mean over ALL children in `wide`.
# 2. Compute the age-14 mean over the COMPLETERS only
#    (the children with dropout == FALSE).
# The last line prints both; note which is smaller.

# Replace each NULL with your code:
mean_all <- NULL
mean_completers <- NULL

if (is.null(mean_all) || is.null(mean_completers)) stop("Replace the NULLs above with your code.")
round(c(all_children = mean_all, completers_only = mean_completers), 2)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mar"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

Subset a column with a logical vector: the completers' values are
`wide$age14[!wide$dropout]`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mar"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

```r
mean_all <- mean(wide$age14)
mean_completers <- mean(______)

round(c(all_children = mean_all, completers_only = mean_completers), 2)
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_mar"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean_all <- mean(wide$age14)
mean_completers <- mean(wide$age14[!wide$dropout])

round(c(all_children = mean_all, completers_only = mean_completers), 2)
```

The completers-only mean is more than a millimeter too low (about 24.9 vs the
true 26.1): we removed exactly the largest children.
:::
:::

Now the Ch. 4 payoff. A likelihood-based model fit to **all available rows**
still uses the dropouts' age 8-12 records, and those records tell the model that
the missing children were large and growing. Watch it repair most of the damage:

```{webr}
#| caption: "[6C] Follow along: likelihood-based analysis of the observed data"
obs <- dental |>
  mutate(dropout = id %in% wide$id[wide$dropout]) |>
  filter(!(dropout & age == 14))

fit_obs <- gls(distance ~ age * gender, data = obs,
               correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))

newdat <- data.frame(age = 14,
                     gender = factor(c("Girl", "Boy"),
                                     levels = c("Girl", "Boy")))
pred <- predict(fit_obs, newdat)
model_based <- sum(pred * prop.table(table(dental_raw$gender))[c("F", "M")])

round(c(true_mean       = mean(wide$age14),
        completers_only = mean(wide$age14[!wide$dropout]),
        model_based     = model_based), 2)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint 6b

1. The mechanism is MAR, yet the completers-only mean was badly biased. Reconcile
   those two facts.
2. Why does the GLS fit on the observed rows do so much better?
3. Would this repair still work if children had dropped out based on how their
   (never-measured) age-14 distance *would have* turned out?
:::


# Wrap-up

You reshaped a real longitudinal file, saw
tracking in the trajectories, measured a within-child correlation near 0.6 with
no decay pattern, fit GLS with compound symmetry and discovered that OLS
standard errors are wrong in *both* directions, used ML for a likelihood ratio
test (boys grow about 0.3 mm per year faster, p = 0.013) and REML for the
reported fit, then ran a MAR experiment showing why the analysis model must use
the variables that drive missingness.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exit questions (do these before you leave)

1. Your collaborator says: "I'll just run `lm()` on the long data; with 108 rows
   the standard errors will be fine." What one thing do you check about a
   covariate before predicting whether its OLS SE is too small or too large?
2. You want to compare `distance ~ age` with `distance ~ age + gender` by LRT
   using `gls()`. What single argument must you add to both calls?
3. A child misses a visit because the previous visit's recorded value exceeded a
   referral threshold. MCAR, MAR, or MNAR?
:::
